summary:
Atacama Region stands under Chile's national legal framework. Outright International's Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, records no Atacama-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding and no division-level information, so the region is assessed at the national score and a visitor's expectations are set by national law rather than by regional ordinance.

That framework is comparatively developed. Legal gender recognition has operated on a self-determination basis since 2019 with no medical or surgical conditions attached; same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022; civil unions since 2015; and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences. Birth certificates have offered a third sex option since 2006, for intersex children. A trans visitor's documents can therefore be aligned to their identity before travel.

Detention carries specific guarantees. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol requiring recognition of a trans detainee's assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, rules on entry examinations and access for trans visitors, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitoring implementation.

The policy record has stalled at national level. The Chilean congress excluded the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombuds for children. Movilh's XXIV Annual Human Rights Report describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers, and a Chilean advocacy group's assessment judged 2024 a year of regression, the first such reversal since 1990.

Documented anti-trans violence remains a live risk. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours, a case treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held for close to an hour at a hotel in Santiago in a transphobic attack during which the assailant said he wanted to kill the victim. Institutional hostility is visible in state employment too: Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging reassignment to administrative duties, exposure of her private life without consent and denial of support.

Regional incident volume is mid-range and rising. Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025, published March 2026) places Atacama at 1.83% of nationally documented abuse cases, a year-on-year rise of 7.69%, within a national pattern in which 14 of 16 regions increased.
tangentialFactors:
Nationally the picture is one of expanding recorded incidence rather than contracting risk. Movilh counts a record 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, up 27.1% and the highest total in 24 years. Only Valparaíso (-17.56%) and Metropolitana (-14.35%) fell; the other 14 regions rose. The report reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate, which is the context in which Atacama's increase should be read.

Two region-specific positives are recorded in the same report. The Municipality of Atacama convened the commune's first Pride march, and Atacama and Puerto Varas became the first regions to hold Pride marches during 2025, extending the movement's territorial visibility. Public visibility of this kind has not so far translated into a fall in documented cases in the region.

Chile's trajectory compares unfavourably with its own recent history. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment treated 2024 as the first year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction.
localsOnly:
Residents of Atacama Region report and document abuse through the national channels Movilh aggregates; the region accounted for 1.83% of nationally documented cases in 2025, a 7.69% rise on the prior year.

The exclusion of the Gender Identity Support Program (PAIG) from the 2026 budget bill is a resident-facing service question, since PAIG is the administrative route through which gender marker changes are processed. Civil society groups and the national ombuds for children have publicly condemned the exclusion.

Local authorities have taken visible steps: the Municipality of Atacama convened the commune's first Pride march, and the region held Pride marches during 2025 alongside Puerto Varas.

Trans residents in state employment face documented institutional hostility nationally, illustrated by Isabella Panes's 2025 lawsuit against Carabineros alleging reassignment, non-consensual exposure of her private life and denial of support.
outOfScopeNotes:
The 2024 regional share used for year-on-year comparison is not reproduced in the 2025 edition of Movilh's report, so the prior-year baseline behind the 7.69% figure is unresolved and cannot be verified from the source.

Outright International's Chile dossier contains no Atacama-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding and no division-level information; the absence of a regional finding is a limit of the source, not evidence that no regional incidents occurred.

Whether the Gendarmería trans-detention protocol is applied in practice in Atacama's detention facilities is not sourced here; only the national protocol and its monitoring committee are documented.

Enforcement outcomes for the 2021 Santiago hotel attack and the 2023 killing of Ever are not stated in the inventory, and no Atacama-specific violence case is recorded.
